newsitem.title: CANADA: Winnipeg braces as Red River crests at Canada border.
newsitem.headline: Winnipeg braces as Red River crests at Canada border.

text.p: The forcible evacuation of 400 people in southern Manitoba was being carried out on Sunday, the last of 17,000 residents who two days ago were ordered to high ground, Canadian officials said.

All residents of southern Manitoba who defied Friday's evacuation order were told they would be forcibly removed by sunset before 37 mph (60 kph) wind gusts on Monday, which were expected to pound large waves against dikes.
Four hundred people had yet to comply and were to be forcibly removed by military helicopter and boats by sunset on Sunday.
Emergency officials raised their peak projections for the Red River by another six inches (15 cm) to 25 feet (7.6 metres).
Dikes were breached at a quarter of the farms in the southern part of the province on Sunday, said Manitoba Emergency Management Organisation executive coordinator Harold Clayton.
Two boys and a man were presumed drowned in the past week's rising waters but no deaths were attributed to the dike breaches, officials said.
"There's about 10 feet (3 metres) of dike built on ice and snow that we're repairing," south Winnipeg resident Greg Arason said.
Dikes built on snow and ice were blamed in part for breaches that forced 90 percent of 50,000 Grand Forks, N.D. residents to evacuate their homes last weekend.
Arason was ordered on Sunday to evacuate his home by Tuesday at noon as were 186 other homeowners on his street.
"We're still optimistic," Arason said as he hauled wood beams to reinforce dikes ringing the Red River oxbow street.
A total 600 riverside homes were ordered evacuated so far in Winnipeg, a city of 650,000, Mayor Susan Thompson said.

Thousands of evacuees sought refuge behind Winnipeg's earthen dike and massive drainage ditch designed to divert the Red River's flood waters. They formed a temporary lake which covered an area twice the size of New York City in southern Manitoba. At its peak it should cover 800 square miles (2,072 sq km).

Farther downstream and just southwest of Winnipeg, 100 earthmoving machines and hundreds of Canadian soldiers raced against the clock to raise a 15 mile (24 km) dike to protect the city as flood water was to within two miles (3 km).
"If the dike breaches, water could reach Winnipeg in four to six hours," Winnipeg Water and Waste engineer Doug McNeil said.

Some 630 amphibious vehicles and high-axle troop carriers were being sent by rail to Winnipeg from a military engineering regiment to evacuate residents living southwest of Winnipeg and in the south of the city, Manitoba Emergency Management Organisation executive coordinator Harold Clayton said.
About 6,700 soldiers should be deployed across southern Manitoba by Tuesday, military officials said.
"All the sandbagging around farm homes is done south of the dike today," 2nd Lt. Martin Coulombe said.
Grand Forks residents were allowed to return to their homes on Sunday and briefly survey the damange.

Upstream at Fargo and nearby Moorhead, Minn., officials said damage could run as high as $7 million, even though that area escaped the massive destuction that hit Grand Forks -- where unofficial estimates have placed damage at as high as $1 billion.
